q: Apple and pear orchards covered a high plateau east of Cape Town long before any vines arrived, and the district is now among the coolest in the country. Which district?
exp: The plateau sits a few hundred metres up, ringed by mountains and open to sea air through a gap, and the rainfall is high. Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Riesling all ripen late there, and the orchards are still the dominant crop.

q: The southernmost vineyards on the African continent stand on a windswept plain near an old mission village, and their Sauvignon Blanc is severe, saline and low-yielding. Which ward?
exp: The ward lies in the Cape Agulhas district with the sea on three sides and almost nothing to break the wind. Crops are tiny because of it, and the wines are correspondingly concentrated and taut.

q: Elgin and Walker Bay both lie within sight of the sea, yet neither of them belongs to the Coastal Region. Which region holds them?
exp: Coastal Region is a name inherited from an older scheme rather than a description of where the districts are, and it covers Stellenbosch, Paarl, Swartland and their neighbours further north. Cape Agulhas, Overberg and Plettenberg Bay sit alongside Elgin and Walker Bay in the southern region.

q: Lime-rich soils are scarce in the Cape and ordinary in one inland district, which used them to breed racehorses long before it used them for Chardonnay. Which district?
exp: Limestone in the ground meant strong bone in the stock, and the same soils now underpin the district's Chardonnay and a great deal of its sparkling wine. Days are hot, but a south-easterly funnels up the valley most afternoons and takes the edge off.

q: Mountains wring the rain out of the westerly weather before it reaches one inland valley, so the vineyards there are irrigated from the river running through them. Which region?
exp: Worcester, Breedekloof and Robertson are its districts, and between them they grow an enormous share of the national crop. Much of it goes to distillation or to everyday blends, but the cooler margins and the older Chenin blocks have changed how the region is read.

q: Semi-desert country beyond the mountain passes grows Touriga Nacional and Tinta Barocca for the Cape's finest fortified reds. Which town sits at the centre of that trade?
exp: The Klein Karoo is hot, dry and stony, which is close enough to the Douro that the Portuguese varieties behave as they should. The same district makes a great deal of fortified Muscadel, red and white, in a sweeter and simpler register.

q: A Cape fortified red left in cask until it turns amber and tastes of nuts and dried fruit is sold under which name?
exp: The Cape prefix replaced a borrowed Portuguese term under an agreement with the European Union, and the family of names maps onto the styles it names. Cape Ruby is young and fruity, and Cape Vintage comes from a single year and does its ageing in the bottle rather than in wood.

q: A Cape grape name translates as cock's foot, after the splayed shape of the bunch. Which name is it?
exp: Hanepoot is Muscat of Alexandria, grown for the table, for raisins and for sweet fortified jerepigo. Muscadel is the Cape name for the other Muscat, the small-berried Muscat de Frontignan, fortified as both a red and a white around Robertson and the Klein Karoo.

q: A cross made at Stellenbosch University in 1925 married a difficult Burgundian red to a hardy southern French workhorse. Which two grapes?
exp: Abraham Perold was after Pinot's flavour with a constitution that could survive the Cape, and the name fuses Pinot with Hermitage, which is what the Cape then called Cinsaut. Nothing was bottled commercially from it until 1961, more than thirty years after the seedlings were planted.

q: Two very different reds reach the shelf under the same Cape variety: one bright, red-fruited and savoury, the other dark and smelling strongly of mocha and chocolate. What produces the second?
opts: Heavily charred oak, used deliberately in the cellar for effect
Fermentation on the skins of a second red variety
Arresting the fermentation with spirit while sugar remains
A much cooler site giving a longer growing season
exp: The mocha style is a cellar decision rather than a vineyard one, built with strongly toasted barrels, staves or chips and often a little sweetness left in. It sells enormously well and it divides opinion, because it tastes more of the treatment than of the grape.

q: A South African red blend earns an informal name of its own when it carries a meaningful share of one home-grown variety. Which variety?
exp: There is no legal definition and producers argue about the proportion, but the presence of the Cape's own crossing is the point of the term. That is precisely what separates it from the other Cape blend, which is built on the red Bordeaux varieties and contains none of it.

q: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot grown at the Cape and bottled together are sold under a borrowed name. Which?
exp: Stellenbosch makes more of it than anywhere else, usually Cabernet-led and firmly structured. Keeping the two Cape blend terms apart is a standard trap: one names the red Bordeaux varieties, the other requires the local crossing.

q: Cape growers called their most widely planted white Steen for generations before anyone connected it to a French variety. Which grape is it?
exp: The identification was made in the 1960s, by which point the grape had been planted for decades on the strength of its yield, its acidity and its usefulness for distillation. It is now the source of the Cape's most distinctive whites, bottled everywhere from fresh and unwooded to barrel-fermented and long-lived.

q: Bush vines planted in the 1960s crop a fraction of what a young trellised block does, and growers pay a premium for their fruit anyway. What do the old vines give?
opts: Riper fruit at lower acidity and higher alcohol
Small, even crops of concentrated fruit
exp: An old vine has a deep root system and has stopped putting energy into growing, so it sets a modest crop and ripens it evenly without much intervention. The Old Vine Project certifies blocks of thirty-five years and older with a seal stating the year they were planted, which gives an old vineyard a documented value it never used to have.

q: A neutral, high-acid white planted across the hot irrigated interior is grown mostly to be distilled rather than drunk as wine. Which variety?
exp: Acidity that survives real heat is exactly what a brandy base needs, and neutrality is a virtue when the still is going to supply the character. South African potstill brandy is a serious category, and the Breede River districts grow most of the wine that goes into it.

q: Cap Classique may be made anywhere in South Africa, from grapes Champagne would never permit. What does the term guarantee instead?
opts: That only Chardonnay and Pinot Noir went into it
That the fruit came from a single registered ward
That the second fermentation happened in the bottle sold
That the wine spent three years in a cellar before release
exp: The term names a method and says nothing about place or variety, which is the reverse of how Champagne is defined. A Cape sparkler made in a pressurised tank is a perfectly legal wine and simply may not use the name.
